content:
Realizing that quantum computing threatens all existing encryption systems is one thing. But what to do about it well, that’s a different beast altogether, and the one that ensnares almost all organizations. At this stage, the threat itself is well documented but turning that awareness into an actual sequenced action plan is where preparations usually come to a standstill. Firms that view quantum readiness as an abstract, long-term concern, rather than as a phased portfolio, achieve far less than firms working from a roadmap.

The good news is that you do not need to invent this roadmap completely from scratch. For years, governments, standards bodies and security researchers have worked on structured methodologies for exactly this problem and they’ve converged on fairly consistent steps that organizations of virtually any size can tailor to suit their own environment.

Step 1: Create a crypto repository

Getting oriented around quantum computing security preparedness steps starts with an unglamorous but essential first step: figuring out where cryptography actually lives across an organization’s systems. This is where almost all credible quantum preparation frameworks begin, because it is truly tough to safeguard what has not been identified. This inventory should include obvious locations such as the encryption protecting external communications and data at rest, but also less obvious places like cryptography baked into old legacy software, hardware, firmware and third-party services.

It is at this step that many organizations discover a world of complexity that is more than meets the eye. Cryptographic implementations often evolve over the course of years (even decades), and usually nobody has an overview of all the places where a vulnerable algorithm might be sneaking in undetected. If you treat this discovery phase as thorough instead of a quick checklist, the payoffs in subsequent steps are substantial.

Step 2: Prioritize by risk and data shelf-life

After the inventory, triage is next. All systems are not created equal and organizations that try to do it all at once invariably will be under pressure from stakeholders and ultimately hit a wall. Data that benefits from a long confidentiality requirement (e.g. a financial record, health information or industrial trade secret) deserves to be looked at more urgently than data with short useful lifespans: since the harvest now, decrypt later risk applies most acutely to information which needs to remain confidential many years into the future.

Also, systems that support critical infrastructure or processes particularly sensitive transactions are generally deserving of earlier priority due both to the potential severity of compromise and, more recently, newly emerging regulatory expectations in sectors such as finance and healthcare.

Step 3: Do Vendor-Level Engagement and Dependency Analysis

Few organizations exercise direct control over all the relevant cryptography impacting their operations. A lot of it lives in vendor products, cloud services and third-party platforms. This renders vendor engagement a key, often undervalued area of the roadmap. Some organizations need to know which vendors have current quantum migration plans, which are still working on a strategy and where dependencies can create potential bottlenecks in the future.

This step also brings up where an organization has less control than it may think. If a migration plan for an internally managed system does not account for third-party dependencies, it creates sizeable gaps that become apparent much later in the process.

Step 4: Create a Phase-wise Migration Plan

Once you understand your inventory, prioritization, and vendor dependencies, the next step is to build an actual migration timeline. The sequence of work described in this plan should first make practical considerations over time, using the key systems identified in step two as a basis for sequencing with a long transition path where quantum-resistant and traditional cryptography will be used alongside fairly seamlessly.

This same way of thinking in phases is reflected in structured national guidance. One of these phased approaches, which is at the same time cross-organizational and cross-country in scale, is represented by coordinated European guidance on this transition (including a coordinated transition roadmap elaborated together with member states and presenting multi-year, better-than-greatest-decisions) to identify which cryptographic systems to migrate.

Step 5: Test it thoroughly before using it.

However, rushing quantum-resistant implementations into production without adequate testing carries its own risks, e.g., interoperability failures and a ‘false sense of security’ when misconfigured systems appear secure but do not function as intended. There is a dedicated testing phase that opens up further possibilities; ideally, it will consist of pilot deployments on lower-risk systems before actually touching the most critical infrastructure, helping catch these issues in a controlled manner rather than during a live rollout that impacts core operations.

The testing process provides an additional opportunity to ensure that migrated systems actually use the new cryptographic mechanisms correctly, rather than falling back to older, insecure algorithms due to misconfiguration, without a clear indication.

Step 6: Establish continuous governance and monitoring

There is no one finish line for quantum preparation. Post-migration, are ongoing governance and new systems included in the first rollout? Is cryptographic drift monitored, whereby older algorithms creep in as updates are rolled out or deployed afresh? New standards and guidance What do I keep track of when it comes to changing security postures as quantum-safe evolves across the broader ecosystem?

This continuous nature is well illustrated by coordinated national initiatives. Federal efforts, such as the national post-quantum cryptography program bringing agency and industry together around this change, illustrate that quantum readiness is not a one-off project that will be completed when migration work is done.

Bringing the Roadmap Together

These six steps build on each other, meaning if you skip one and hop to the next like, say, migration without a good inventory being in place first then you can end up creating rework instead of time savings. Organizations that work through this roadmap slowly and steadily, will be in a better position than those who either delay starting completely or fast track through steps with little of the foundational elements developed.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does a cryptographic inventory show up at the outset of any migration work?

If we are not aware of where cryptography is being used throughout an organization’s systems, it will be difficult to prioritize migration and even more challenging to ensure that algorithms known to be vulnerable are not inadvertently left in place simply because they were never discovered.

How do organizations need to prioritize the systems that need migration?

Critical infrastructure and very sensitive transactions with data that needs long-term confidentiality all of which are systems that need to be dedicated earlier, because they have the highest risk regarding presently acquiring an interception (the intercepts today) plus future decryption.

Is quantum preparation ever really finished once migration is complete?

Not entirely. With the evolution of quantum-safe standards, progress on new systems should be monitored and older vulnerable algorithms can easily sneak back in through updates necessitating ongoing governance.
